div.p: Suppose we have a sequence of latent variable \xi = (z_{1}, z_{2}, \ldots , z_{T}) and the corresponding sequence of observations \mathcal {H} = (x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots , x_{T})
div.div: Goal. We want to compute the posterior distribution \mathbb {P}(\xi \mid \mathcal {H}).
div.p: Suppose \mathcal {z} is a discrete random variable taking at most K different values. Then, for horizon length T, there are K^T possible values for \xi . Thus, computing \mathbb {P}(\xi \mid \mathcal {H}) blows up exponentially.
Suppose that z \in \{0, 1\} and T = 2. Then
If T = 3,
If T = 4,
Directly computing the probability for each possible value of \xi would thus take O(K^T) or exponential in the horizon length. Can we do better?
In the particular case of a hidden markov model, we can achieve O(TK^2)!!!

section.p: A hidden markov model is a statistical model, where the hidden states h \in \mathcal {H} form a Markov Chain, such that \mathbb {P}(h_{t+1} \mid h_{1}, \ldots , h_{t}) = \mathbb {P}(h_{t + 1} \mid h_{t})
Unlike a Markov chain, in addition to the hidden states, a hidden markov models contains observations x \in \mathcal {X} with associated emission probabilities \mathbb {P}(x_t \mid h_t).

figure.figcaption: Graphical model of a hidden markov model.

section.p: From the graphical model, we can see that for any i < j, (x_{0}, \ldots , x_i) \perp (x_{j}, \ldots , x_{N}) \mid z_{i}. Or in english, observations are independent conditioned on the hidden state.

div.p: In our setup, we can rewrite the marginal as
From Baye's rule, we can decompose this as
Since we are considering an HMM, (x_{1}, \ldots , x_t) and (x_{t + 1}, \ldots , x_{T}) are conditionally independent conditioned on z_t. Thus, we can further simplify this to
div.code: \mathbb {P}(z_t \mid x_{0}, \ldots , x_{T}) = \frac {\mathbb {P}(x_{t + 1}, \ldots , x_{T} \mid z_t) \mathbb {P}(x_{0}, \ldots , x_{t}, z_t)}{\mathbb {P}(x_{0}, \ldots , x_{T})}
div.div: Notation. We will now consider the terms in the numerator separately. The first can be viewed as the backward term \beta _t(z) = \mathbb {P}(x_{t + 1}, \ldots , x_{T} \mid z_t = z), and the second as the forward term \phi _t(z) = \mathbb {P}(x_{0}, \ldots , x_{t}, z_t = z). Naming convention is to denote which direction in time information propagates (we will see shortly).
Remark. Both passes are O(TK^2) because at each timestep, it requires computing \mathbb {P}(z_{t} \mid z_{t - 1}) or \mathbb {P}(z_{t + 1} \mid z_{t}) which is a K \times K transition matrix.
div.p: Notably, the structure of the HMM ensures each marginal \mathbb {P}(z_t \mid \mathcal {H}) depends only on the local transition probabilities \mathbb {P}(z_{t} \mid z_{t - 1}) and \mathbb {P}(z_{t + 1} \mid z_{t}) rather than the exponential global \mathbb {P}(z_{0}, \ldots , z_{T}). This lends itself to the idea of a dynamic programming algorithm, where we compute the posterior of the preceding / succeeding latent and use the result for the next. Since we have bi-directional dependencies this requires making two passes a forward and backward pass. The key remaining detail is that these components can be efficiently combined to recover the full true marginal.

section.p: Finally, all that remains is to combine \phi and \beta to recover the true posterior. Recall that these directly correspond to the components in the numerator i.e.
Therefore, it remains to compute the normalization term \mathbb {P}(\mathcal {H}). To do so, note that
Thus, the true posterior can be recovered as
Since z is discrete, this sum is only O(K) and therefore easily computable.

div.p: Due to the unstructured nature of PhD life / knowledge work in general, I have been trying to come up with the most effective system to ensure I am Getting Things Doneironically I found this system actually not that helpful.

Since Cal Newport is a professor (can relate to the knowledge work problem), I have been reading a lot of his stuff on productivity. I read Deep Work awhile back and the guiding principles make sense to me. However, I still struggle to actually implement it.
I often refer back to Atomic Habits as it intuitively just makes so much sense to me.

ul.li: Start small: starting a habit should take less than 2 minutes.
Never miss a habit twice.
Habit anchors: I am always going to run so now after I run I stretch, which has resulted in remarkable stretching consistency (see my Weeknotes).
Habit tracking: Something I am also implementing in my Weeknotes with habitify.

section.p: I have been using todoist and habitify. I decided on these tools primarily because of their API availability. I wanted to be able to add / complete / see outstanding tasks or habits for the day without the allure of everything else my browser has to offer. Also visualization for my Weeknotes.

ul.li: I had Claude write a little script to have my next tasks listed when clicked in my status bar, so I do not have to open the browser to check what I need to do today.

section.p: It seems how to properly use these (todoist in particular) is the subject of much debate. Here, I will outline what I converged to / works for ME right now. I have broken down my system into a hierarchy:

ol.li: Higher level: how to actually choose what to do.
Lower level: how to actually do the chosen task.

section.p: This is effectively a task management system.

Work streams. I took this name from my investment banker friends (sounds cool / important). Basically, these are groupings I have made and allocated time for each day. They roughly consist of the following:

ul.li: Research / work (first thing in the morning):
Active work towards new artifact or paper i.e. coding up ideas.
In the absence of ideas, studying existing relevant papers.
Deliberate practice:
Name taken from Cal Newport.
Basically, something I need to understand or master for research that is not novel i.e. writing or optimizing a known kernel.
Extraneous Study:
Things not directly related to research, but I am curious about.
I try to maintain study of related computer science fields. Primarily, studying a textbook in something like OS, computer architecture, etc.
Habits / daily upkeep:
Mainly consists of reviewing Anki cards daily that come from extraneous study / deliberate practice.
Necessary to stay on top of, but it normally takes < 30min if active.

section.p: To decide on the next task, I use a priority-based systemThis idea is mainly based on the MLFQ, which has been proven effective for balancing response / turnaround time:

ol.li: Things I will be working on today / until they are done. At most ONE thing per work stream.
The backlog of things to do next

ul.li: An index to find things to move to priority 1 for the next day
Keep relatively small to avoid the crippling nature of choice - roughly on the order of things I want done this week.

ol.li: A larger backlog of things - should be completed in the next month or so.
Things I am not working on right now, or have any need to be completed any time soon.

section.p: To maintain this system, I have reviews each day and week (tracking with habitify) to make sure I stay consistent.

ul.li: For each work stream,
If I finished the allocated task for the day, get new task from priority 2.
Else, do nothing and continue with the current task.
Review inbox and move new tasks to corresponding work stream for review on Friday.
If immediately important, can move directly to priority 1 / 2.
Look at calendar for next day and timeblock work streams for the next day.
Since PhD work is so hard to predict, I have found timeblocking any further than one day in advance to be a futile effort.
Typically done on Fridays, so that I can dynamically allocate time on weekends if needed.
For each work stream,

ol.li: Look in remaining priority 2 and priority 3 tasks.
Define what I think a successful week would look like (e.g. if I get all these things done next week I will be happy).

ul.li: Look at calendar for week to guide this decision.

ol.li: Get rid of at least two of those tasks (initial plan always too ambitious).
Move / keep remaining tasks in priority 2.

ul.li: Write Weeknotes for the week.

header.h3: What to do when actually working on a task

section.p: This is the harder part (and requires the most discipline). When working on a task, especially a more open-ended one like research, it is very common that a million other things come up that seem immediately important. All of the sudden, you have a great idea for the research project you haven't worked on in months.

It is crucial to collect and forget about these things until they are scheduled. This is the one thing I did take from Getting Things Done. The system should flow like water. Making this achievable is where the todoist API becomes crucial.

ul.li: I have a script bound by dwm that pops up vim for me to write down the task and, on save, it sends it to my inbox in todoist.
I have more involved ones that allow me to actually allocate it to the specific work stream / priority if it is immediately obvious.

section.p: Another thing that I have found useful to actually achieving this watery flow is the pomodoro technique. This basically lets me gaslight myself into thinking I can go to the other things as soon as the timer ends (which is intentionally always just close enough). By the end, I often no longer have this urge and can continue on the scheduled tasks.

div.p: This will be a brief tour through all the fundamentals needed to understand the first instantiation of FlashAttention as introduced in FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness.

section.p: This covers the math behind the online softmax algorithm required by Flash Attention (v1).
The first thing we must consider is numerical precision. Namely, the original softmax operation is given by
However, when operating with low precision data types (i.e. float16) the maximum value is 65536. Therefore, with \exp we can easily get numerically overflow.

To get around this, the online softmax algorithm adheres to the safe softmax. For safe softmax, we simply multiply the numerator and denominator by \exp (-m), where m = \max \{x_{1}, \ldots , x_n\}. This gives
Since x_i - m \leq 0, this ensures that each \exp (x_i - m) is bounded in a safe range.
section.div: Problem. Note that computing the \max over \mathbf {x} means that we must have all of the logits in a row of QK^T materialized in SMEM, or first loop over all of them to compute the max before computing the normalization constant.

section.p: The online softmax algorithm fuses the max reduction into the normalization pass, so a single sweep over the row suffices to compute the normalization with the max. The key difficulty is that the denominator depends on n for each i i.e.

Therefore, we must find a recursive relationship such that d_{i+1} = f(d_i, m_i, x_{i+1}) for some function f. This would then allow us to locally compute d_{i+1} with only the local information of current x_{i+1} and the two running statistics d_i and m_i. This is exactly the kind of algorithm that is conducive to memory tiling.
section.div: Question. What is f(d_i, m_i, x_{i+1})?

div.details:
Proof. This can be seen by directly rewriting d_{i + 1}.
\begin {align*} d_{i + 1} &= \sum _{j = 1}^{i+1} \exp (x_j - m_{i + 1}) \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{i} \exp (x_j - m_{i+1})\right ) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{i} \exp (x_j - m_{i})\right )\exp (m_{i} - m_{i + 1}) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \\ &= d_{i} \exp (m_{i} - m_{i + 1}) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \end {align*}

section.p: The running denominator d is rescaled by e^{m - m_{\text {new}}} each time a new maximum is found, keeping it consistent with the safe-softmax shift.

pre.code: m = float("-inf") # running max of the logits d = 0.0 # running softmax denominator for i in range(n): # one fused sweep for the stats m_new = max(m, x[i]) d = d * exp(m - m_new) + exp(x[i] - m_new) m = m_new p = [exp(x[i] - m) / d for i in range(n)] # second pass: normalized probs

section.div: Remark. Unfortunately, we cannot get around the second pass to compute the normalized output for \mathbf {p}. However, this is not the case in Flash Attention (v1).

section.p: Unlike in the online softmax, we are not interested in the outputted probability vector \mathbf {p}. Instead we are interested in the entire output matrix O given by
For more details see self-attention.
section.div: Notation. In correspondence with the notation in the online softmax, we define the following: x_{i,j} = \mathbf {q}_i \cdot \mathbf {k}_j, where \mathbf {q}_i is the ith row of Q and \mathbf {k}_j is the jth row of K. Similarly, \mathbf {o}_i is the ith row of the output matrix O given by \mathbf {o}_i = \sum _{j = 1}^{n} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_n)}{d_n} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j
section.p: Now following the template provided by the online softmax, we must find a recurrence for \mathbf {o}_i. Namely, we will consider the sequence \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' given by \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' = \sum _{j = 1}^{k} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j, such that \mathbf {o}_{i,n}' = \mathbf {o}_n
section.div:
Claim. We have the following recurrence for \mathbf {o}_{i,k}':
\mathbf {o}_{i,k}' = \mathbf {o}_{i, k-1} \cdot \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k

div.details:
Proof. We will proceed by directly rewriting the recurrence for \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' as
\begin {align*} \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' &= \sum _{j = 1}^{k} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{k - 1} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_{k-1})}{d_{k-1}} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j\right ) \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,k} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k \\ &= \mathbf {o}_{i, k-1} \cdot \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,k} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k .\end {align*}

section.p: Thus, we are left with the following algorithm

pre.code: for i in range(N): # one query row at a time m = float("-inf") # running max of the logits d = 0.0 # running softmax denominator o = zeros(head_dim) # running output accumulator for j in range(M): # stream over keys/values x = q[i] @ k[j] # logit x_{i,j} m_new = max(m, x) d_new = d * exp(m - m_new) + exp(x - m_new) o = o * (d * exp(m - m_new) / d_new) + (exp(x - m_new) / d_new) * v[j] m, d = m_new, d_new out[i] = o

section.div: Remark. A key benefit of this algorithm is that it is entirely parallelizable across rows. This means that we can loop across entire tiles like in the GEMM case.

section.p: The forward pass of flash attention avoids materializing the N \times N attention matrix by streaming an online softmax. The backward pass has to pull the same trick twice over, because the naive gradient computation wants two N \times N matrices — \mathbf {P} and d\mathbf {P}. Getting there means first writing down every gradient we need, then finding a way to recompute rather than store each one.
section.div: Notation. Following the notation in the original paper, \mathbf {S} = \mathbf {Q} \mathbf {K}^T, \quad \mathbf {P} = \mathrm {softmax}(\mathbf {S}), \quad \mathbf {O} = \mathbf {P} \mathbf {V}, where \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {V}, \mathbf {O} are N \times d and \mathbf {S}, \mathbf {P} are N \times N. For a scalar loss \phi we abbreviate the gradient with respect to any matrix \mathbf {X} as d\mathbf {X} = \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {X}}, and write \mathbf {L}_i for the softmax denominator of row i saved by the forward pass, so that \mathbf {P}_{ij} = \exp (\mathbf {Q}_i \cdot \mathbf {K}_j) / \mathbf {L}_i.

header.h3: The gradients we need for FlashAttention

section.p: Everything downstream is chain rule; the only step with any content is differentiating through the softmax. We take the gradients in dependency order, starting from d\mathbf {O} which arrives from the layer above.
Both fall straight out of the product rule for matrices:

The shapes are a useful sanity check. d\mathbf {O} has one entry per output, so it is N \times d; \mathbf {V}^T is d \times N; their product is N \times N, matching \mathbf {P}. Likewise \mathbf {P}^T d\mathbf {O} is N \times d, matching \mathbf {V}.
Componentwise, from \mathbf {O}_{ik} = \sum _j \mathbf {P}_{ij} \mathbf {V}_{jk},
That last line is worth noting already: d\mathbf {V} never needs \mathbf {P} stored, only the ability to re-evaluate \mathbf {P}_{ij} from \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, and \mathbf {L}.

Softmax acts row by row, so drop into the scalar case with \mathbf {s} and \mathbf {p} single rows. The softmax Jacobian is \partial \mathbf {p}_i / \partial \mathbf {s}_j = \mathbf {p}_i(\delta _{ij} - \mathbf {p}_j), giving

As a row vector this is d\mathbf {s} = \mathbf {p} \odot (d\mathbf {p} - \mathbf {p} \cdot d\mathbf {p}), where the subtracted term is the scalar \mathbf {p} \cdot d\mathbf {p} broadcast across the row. Collecting those scalars into a column \mathbf {D} with \mathbf {D}_i = \mathbf {P}_i \cdot d\mathbf {P}_i recovers the matrix form
\mathbf {D} is the piece that will cause trouble later: it is a dot product over an entire row of \mathbf {P}, which is exactly the thing we refuse to materialize.
One more chain rule, and the sums run over opposite indices:

Every gradient above is expressed through \mathbf {P}_{ij} and d\mathbf {P}_{ij}, both N \times N. Materializing either one is exactly the quadratic memory cost the forward pass went to such lengths to avoid, so the backward pass has to be able to produce those entries on demand.
section.div: Insight. Both are recoverable from the N \times d tensors already resident in memory. The forward pass saved \mathbf {L}, so \mathbf {P}_{ij} = \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}}, and d\mathbf {P} is just an inner product of two rows, d\mathbf {P}_{ij} = \sum _{k} d\mathbf {O}_{ik} \mathbf {V}_{jk} = d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {V}_j. Neither ever requires an N \times N intermediate.
section.p: Substituting both into the previous section leaves d\mathbf {Q} and d\mathbf {K} in terms of \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {V}, d\mathbf {O}, \mathbf {L}, and \mathbf {D} alone:

One problem survives. \mathbf {D}_i = \mathbf {P}_i \cdot d\mathbf {P}_i is a dot product over a full row, so computing it inside the streaming loop would mean a reduction over all j before any tile of d\mathbf {Q}_i could be finished. This is the same global dependency the online softmax was designed to break.
The way out is that the row sum has already been computed once, in the forward pass. Expanding and pulling d\mathbf {O}_i out of the sum:

The inner sum is precisely the definition of \mathbf {O}_i. So \mathbf {D} is a single elementwise product of d\mathbf {O} and \mathbf {O} summed along the head dimension — one O(Nd) pass over tensors we already have, done once before the backward loop begins.
Forward pass. Store \mathbf {O} and the softmax denominators \mathbf {L}, both O(Nd).
Between the passes. Receive d\mathbf {O} from the layer above (automatic in JAX), then precompute \mathbf {D}_i = d\mathbf {O}_i \cdot \mathbf {O}_i in O(N) memory.
Backward pass. Stream over tiles, recomputing \mathbf {P}_{ij} from \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {L} and d\mathbf {P}_{ij} from d\mathbf {O}, \mathbf {V} as needed:

ol.li: d\mathbf {V}_j = \sum _i \mathbf {P}_{ij} d\mathbf {O}_i, accumulated over query tiles.
d\mathbf {Q}_i = \sum _j \mathbf {P}_{ij}(d\mathbf {O}_i \cdot \mathbf {V}_j - \mathbf {D}_i)\mathbf {K}_j, accumulated over key tiles.
d\mathbf {K}_j = \sum _i \mathbf {P}_{ij}(d\mathbf {O}_i \cdot \mathbf {V}_j - \mathbf {D}_i)\mathbf {Q}_i, accumulated over query tiles.

section.p: Each accumulator is O(d) per row or column, so the whole backward pass stays linear in N.

header.h2: The running max makes the chunk merge exact

section.p: In flash attention, what running statistics travel between KV chunks, and how are two chunks merged?

div.details:
Answer Each query block carries three: M, the running maximum of q \cdot k; L, the running softmax denominator; and O, the running output.
Merging chunks with local maxima M^1, M^2 and sums L^1, L^2 rescales each to the shared maximum:
L = e^{M^1 - \max (M^1, M^2)}L^1 + e^{M^2 - \max (M^1, M^2)}L^2
This is exact, not an approximation. It is only \sum _i e^{a_i + b} = e^b \sum _i e^{a_i}: pulling a constant out of a sum of exponentials. The maximum is subtracted for numerical stability and put back by the same identity — see Online Softmax for the one-pass version of the argument.
The payoff is memory, not FLOPs. The [B,T,S,N] attention matrix is never materialised, so memory is O(1) in the number of chunks while the FLOP count stays quadratic. The query block sits in VMEM and only the KV chunks stream in, which is also what raises the arithmetic intensity.

div.p: Murphi is an explicit-state model checker: you describe a system as guarded transition rules, state the invariants, and it enumerates every reachable interleaving looking for a violation. That makes it a natural fit for cache coherence, where the steady-state behavior is easy and the races are not. This post builds a directory-based MESI protocol in Murphi, starting from MSI and adding state every time the checker finds a way to break it.

The state tables come from A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence, which doubles as the source for these notes. The recurring lesson is that the published tables are not quite enough: every protocol below needs transient states the tables leave implicit.

section.p: Syntactical things I need to remember from Murphi docs. Most things are straightforward, but there are a few things to note:
A declaration is a variable or a collection of variables that are used in the rules.
A rule is a transition from one state to another

ul.li: Each rule can optionally have an initial condition required to be fired
We can easily define rules for all the processors or collection of n things with ruleset.
For our use case, rules are used to define

ol.li: Controller actions
Receiving a request from the network
Retrying stalled requests

section.p: A startstate is the intial configuration for all our declarations.
An invariant is something that Murphi checks to ensure is true at all possible configurations of the system.

ol.li: Find all rules whose conditions are true in the current state. (i.e. conditional expressions are true, given the current values of the global variables).
Choose one arbitrarily and execute the action, yielding a new state.

section.p: The valid-invalid protocol shipped with the Murphi docs uses two Virtual Channels. A directory protocol needs three: one each for requests, forwarded requests, and responses. The reason is that deadlock is a cycle in the dependency graph, so it suffices to exhibit one.

ul.li: A node issues GetS to the directory, giving an edge N_1 \to D.
The directory forwards Fwd-GetS to the owner, extending the chain to N_1 \to D \to N_2.
The owner sends data back to the requester, closing the cycle N_1 \to D \to N_2 \to N_1.

section.p: The data closing that cycle would travel on the same channel as the requests waiting behind it, so a full request buffer wedges the response that would drain it. Partitioning by message class breaks the cycle:

ul.li: Request: GetS, GetM, PutS, PutM
Forwarded: Fwd-GetS, Fwd-GetM, Inv, PutAck
Response: Data, InvAck

section.p: These are enumerated directly in the model's MessageType.
MESI is easier to reach through MSI, where there is less to get wrong and the races are already interesting enough.
The starting point is the primer's MSI cache controller table.

figure.figcaption: MSI cache controller, requests and forwards. Rows are states, columns are events, and each cell reads action/next state: \to is "send to", a bare is "no action", an absent next state means "stay put", and a shaded cell is one the table leaves empty.

section.p: The response arrivals split off into their own table, because only a transient state can be waiting on one.

figure.figcaption: MSI cache controller, responses. Data comes from the directory unless the column says otherwise; the stable states are omitted, since none of them can be waiting on a response.

section.p: Several entries here are left blank; those are resolved at runtime from the AckCount, which is why the per-processor record carries an ack field alongside the state.
section.div: Remark. load, store, and replacement only move the protocol between stable states. To simulate the system it is therefore enough to implement the rules that initiate those transitions evict from modified, load from invalid, and let the model checker drive the transient states from there.

section.p: The directory side starts from the analogous table.

tr.td: data → Req, add Req to Sharers / S
data → Req, add Req to Sharers
data → Req, Inv → Sharers, clear Sharers, Owner := Req / M
Fwd-GetS → Owner, add Owner + Req to Sharers, clear Owner / S^D

figure.figcaption: MSI directory controller, coherence requests. The italicized clear Owner in M/GetS is the table's, and is wrong (see below).

tr.td: remove Req from Sharers, Put-Ack → Req
remove Req from Sharers, Put-Ack → Req / I
remove Req from Sharers, Put-Ack → Req
data → memory, clear Owner, Put-Ack → Req / I
remove Req from Sharers, Put-Ack → Req
remove Req from Sharers, Put-Ack → Req
remove Req from Sharers, Put-Ack → Req

figure.figcaption: MSI directory controller, evictions and data. A PutM always carries the line with it; one from a node that is not the current owner is stale and needs only an acknowledgment.

section.p: This table is where the first real gap shows up. It gives the directory a single transient state, and the races below force a second one, M^D.

header.h3: Losing data to a PutM/Fwd-GetM race

section.p: Consider the PutM rule that downgrades a cache from modified to invalid. The evicting cache must not drop the data when it sends PutM, because it may still have to service a forwarded request; it transitions to MI^A and keeps the value. But nothing stops the PutAck from arriving first, taking it to I before the Fwd-GetM shows up. The data is gone and the forwarded request has nobody to answer it.

Fix. Add the M^D state to the directory controller. While in M^D, a PutM from a node that is not the current owner stalls until the data arrives. Leaving M^D for M requires the new owner to send data back to the directory even on a three-hop transaction, so the directory learns that the forward actually completed. I have not found a cleaner way to close this race without the extra state.

header.h3: Deadlocking two stores against a load

section.p: The M^D fix introduces a deadlock of its own. Take two processors that store-miss and a third that load-misses. The second store wins at the directory: the first store gets data and moves IM^{AD} \to IM^{A}, then the second triggers a Fwd-GetM that takes ownership away from it.

Meanwhile the load miss sits in IS^D. When its Inv arrives, the table says to stall — and because Inv and Fwd-GetM share the forwarded channel, that stall blocks the Fwd-GetM behind it. The winning processor never receives the data, and nothing ever drains the channel.

Fix. Another transient state absent from the table: II^A, meaning "was in IS^A, got invalidated, now waiting on PutAck before settling in I". The invalidation is processed rather than stalled, so the forwarded channel keeps moving.

header.h3: Not clearing the owner too eagerly

section.p: One more correction to the table: when the home directory is in M and receives a GetS, it must not clear the owner field as the figure directs. Once in S^D, the directory can no longer tell whether an incoming PutM came from the owner (and should stall) or from a stale node. The owner is only cleared once the data has actually arrived.
With those states in place the rest of MSI is mechanical, and MESI is a short step from it (modulo two design choices and two more races).

figure.figcaption: MESI cache controller, requests and forwards. Bold marks what MESI adds to MSI here, the E and EI^A rows.
MESI cache controller, responses, again over the transient states only. The whole of MESI's addition here is one cell: ExclusiveData landing in IS^D gives E instead of S.

section.p: Silent upgrades. If a cache in E may upgrade to M silently, the directory never learns the line went dirty, and the value it hands to the next GetS or GetM is stale. There are two consistent ways out: forbid the silent upgrade, in which case no forwarding is needed; or allow it and treat E exactly like M, forwarding everything. Neither requires a writeback on PutE. I take the first, matching the table.

Signaling exclusivity. The directory needs a way to tell a requester "you are the first reader, take the line exclusive." That is a new ExclusiveData message: receiving it in IS^D lands the cache in E rather than S. It turns out to also be the key to the second race below.
section.div: Remark. Once PutE or PutM has been sent, EI^A and MI^A are functionally identical. Both appear above for completeness, but transitioning from E straight into MI^A verifies the same.

section.p: Symmetrically, the directory gains an E^D state, which for completeness is kept distinct from M^D but could be folded into it.

The first processor issues GetS and waits in IS^D, while the home directory has already moved to E and sent it ExclusiveData. A second processor then issues GetM, and home's Fwd-GetM overtakes the data in flight.
Fix. Stall Fwd-GetM and Fwd-GetS in IS^D until the data lands. This is safe here because the data is on the response channel, which no stall can block.

header.h3: Losing exclusive data to an invalidation

section.p: The nastier version of the same race: the invalidation arrives before the forward. By the II^A rule inherited from MSI, a PutAck in that state drops the line to I. This discards data a forwarded request is about to ask for.

ol.li: Proc_1 load-misses → IS^D
Home takes the first GetS from Proc_1 → E, sends ExclusiveData
Proc_2 issues GetM → IM^{AD}
Home sends Inv to Proc_1
Home forwards Fwd-GetM to Proc_1
Proc_1 receives Inv → II^D
Proc_1 receives ExclusiveData → I, and the data is lost

section.p: Fix. ExclusiveData pays for itself a second time. Because the message is distinguishable from ordinary Data, a cache receiving it in II^D knows it was the first reader and transitions to E instead of I. There, the pending Fwd-GetM or Fwd-GetS is handled correctly.
Folding all of the above in leaves these two state machines, which Murphi verifies exhaustively.

div.div: Remark. Note that the gradient is with respect to \theta , where \theta is just the third argument to \mathsf {ELBO} as defined above. Notably, \theta _t will show up elsewhere later but will NOT be backpropagated through.

section.p: The above motivates the expectation step of the EM algorithm. Namely how can we compute the lower bound expectation for the best possible q.

Recall (or review) from the discussion on ELBO that q(z) = p(z | x; \theta ) maximizes the ELBO for a given x and \theta . Therefore, we actually want to learn q_{\phi }(z, x, \theta ) \approx p(z | x; \theta ). To do so, we can simply maximize the ELBO (duh). Formally, \phi _{t+1} = \argmax _{\phi } \mathbb {E}_{x \sim \mathcal {D}, z \sim q}\left [\log \frac {p(x, Z; \theta _t)}{q_{\phi }(Z, x, \theta _t)}\right ]
section.div: Question. Now this is all cool theoretically but how TF do we actually maximize this thing?

div.details: Answer. It is highly dependent on the parametrization of p and q.

div.p:
We define the problem as
p(z) \sim N(0, 1)
p(x | z; \theta ) \sim N(\mu _{\theta }(z), \sigma _{\theta }(z))
q_{\phi }(z | x, \theta ) \sim N(\mu _{\phi }(x), \sigma _\phi (x)) where \mu _{\{\phi , \theta \}}, \sigma _{\{\phi , \theta \}} are parametrized neural networks. Then we can rewrite the ELBO as (ignoring constants)
\begin {align*} \mathsf {ELBO}(x, q, \theta ) &= \mathbb {E}_{x \sim \mathcal {D}, z \sim q(\cdot \mid x, \theta )} \left [\log p(Z) - \log \frac {p(x \mid Z; \theta )}{q_{\phi }(Z, x, \theta )}\right ] \\ &= \mathbb {E}_{x \sim \mathcal {D}, z \sim q(\cdot \mid x, \theta )} \left [-\frac {Z^2}{2} - \frac {\sigma _{\phi }(x)^2}{\sigma _{\theta }(z)^2}\big ((Z - \mu _{\theta }(Z))^2 - (Z - \mu _{\phi }(x))^2\big )\right ] .\end {align*}

section.div: Problem. We need to sample realization z \sim q_{\phi }(\cdot |x, \theta ). So isn't our realization z a function of \phi . How would we optimize this?
section.p: Now for a given sample x_i \sim \mathcal {D}, we can get a sample z_i(\phi ) \sim q(\cdot \mid x_i, \theta ) that is differentiable with respect to \phi . Using this, we can get the stochastic gradient estimate \nabla _q \widetilde {\mathsf {ELBO}}(x, q, \theta ) = \nabla _{\phi } \left [\frac {z_i(\phi )^2}{2} - \frac {\sigma _{\phi }(x)^2}{\sigma _{\theta }(z)^2}\big ((z_i(\phi ) - \mu _{\theta }(z_i(\phi )))^2 - (z_i(\phi ) - \mu _{\phi }(x))^2\big )\right ]

Finally, we have reached the maximization step. This step is fairly straightforward after all the progress we have made. Once we have a tight lower bound i.e. q(z) \approx p(z \mid x; \theta ) then we simply fix q and maximize the ELBO for \theta i.e. in the above example and algorithm we instead compute \nabla _\theta \widetilde {\mathsf {ELBO}}(x, q, \theta ) = \nabla _{\theta } \left [\frac {z_i(\phi )^2}{2} - \frac {\sigma _{\phi }(x)^2}{\sigma _{\theta }(z)^2}\big ((z_i(\phi ) - \mu _{\theta }(z_i(\phi )))^2 - (z_i(\phi ) - \mu _{\phi }(x))^2\big )\right ] Alternating between these steps yields the expectation-maximization algorithm the ML oldheads mythologize.

div.p: Setup. We are given a joint distribution p(X, Z; \theta ), where X and Z are random variables with their joint parametrized by \theta . We are also given a dataset \mathcal {D} containing realizations of only X i.e. Z is a latent random variable.
div.div: Goal. We want to learn p(x; \theta ).
div.p: However, p(x; \theta ) = \int p(x, z; \theta ) \mathrm {d}z = \int p(x | z; \theta )p(z) \mathrm {d}z, which is computationally intractable for most continuous Z.
div.div: Question. Can we update \theta for a given realization of x and z?
div.p:
Motivation. Suppose we had some q(z) that we could sample realizations of Z from. Then we want to find some reasonable \ell _{\theta }, such that \theta ^* \approx \arg \max _{\theta } \mathbb {E}_{x, \sim p(x; \theta ^*), z \sim q(z)}[\ell _{\theta }(X, Z)]
Remark. q(z) can potentially (and will) depend on the sample x_i. This is OK because we are given x_i's, which we can then just pass to q to get the corresponding z_i.
Why is this the case? Because then (for well-behaved \ell _{\theta }) \theta _{t + 1} = \theta _{t} - \alpha \nabla _{\theta _{t}}\ell _{\theta _{t}}(x_i, z_i) \to \theta ^* i.e. SGD is a reasonable thing to do, where the gradient is for a single sample of x_i and z_i which we have readily available from our dataset \mathcal {D} and our distribution q that we can sample from. This idea comes up a lot in optimization, such as the \log trick in the original policy gradient.

Similar to the \log trick, the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) comes from a simple multiply and divide trick. Namely, \begin {align*} \log p(x; \theta ) &= \log \int p(x, z; \theta ) \mathrm {d}z \\ &= \log \int p(x, z; \theta ) \frac {q(z)}{q(z)} \mathrm {d}z \\ &= \log \mathbb {E}_{z \sim q(z)} \frac {p(x, Z; \theta )}{q(z)} \\ &\geq \mathbb {E}_{z \sim q(z)} \log \frac {p(x, Z; \theta )}{q(z)} .\end {align*} The last inequality follows directly from Jensen's Inequality. However, note that this is only a lower bound and therefore not exactly what we want. For example, if we were to pick q \sim N(0, 1) and then optimize the ELBO for \theta we would not necessarily find a good \theta for the likelihood \log p(x; \theta ). Luckily, we can actually get the difference \log p(x; \theta ) - ELBO in closed form! Namely, \begin {align*} \log p(x; \theta ) - \mathrm {ELBO} &= \log p(x; \theta ) - \mathbb {E}_{z \sim q(z)} \log \frac {p(x, Z; \theta )}{q(z)} \\ &= \int \left (\log p(x; \theta ) - \log \frac {p(x, z; \theta )}{q(z)}\right )q(z) \\ &= \int \left (\log \frac {p(x; \theta )q(z)}{p(x, z; \theta )}\right )q(z) \\ &= \int \left (\log \frac {p(x; \theta )q(z)}{p(z | x; \theta )p(x; \theta )}\right )q(z) \\ &= \int \left (\log \frac {q(z)}{p(z | x; \theta )}\right )q(z) \\ &= \mathrm {KL}\big (q(z) \mid \mid p(z | x; \theta )\big ) .\end {align*} Thus, to tighten the lower bound we can optimize q_{\phi }(z) to try to match p(z | x; \theta ). As a sanity check, lets make sure these match when q(z) = p(z \mid x; \theta ). \begin {align*} \mathbb {E}_{z \sim q(z)} \log \frac {p(x, Z; \theta )}{q(z)} &= \int \log \frac {p(x, z; \theta )}{q(z)}\mathrm {d}z \\ &= \int \log \frac {p(x; \theta )p(z \mid x; \theta )}{p(z \mid x; \theta )}\mathrm {d}z \\ &= \int \log p(x; \theta )\mathrm {d}z \\ &= \log (x; \theta ) .\end {align*} You may be wondering how we use this algorithmically to find \theta ^*? This will be the main idea of expectation maximization. Feel free to check it out!

I used LazyVim for a long time, but I kept hitting a wall: understanding how LazyVim did something was consistently harder than if I had just written the thing myself. So I gave myself one day to rebuild from scratch, with the modest goal of first-class support for \TeX , Python, Forester, and C/C++. That one-day sprint is long past, and the config has kept evolving since; this note describes where it landed, not the frantic first pass. The through-line is that almost everything now leans on Neovim's own primitives instead of a framework, which is exactly the transparency I was missing.
div.div: Remark. The whole config lives in my dotfiles. It is a thin init.lua that loads four modules (config.lazy, config.options, config.keymaps, and core.lsp), with the actual plugin specs under lua/plugins/ and per-server LSP tables under lsp/.

section.p: To my surprise, a lot of the behavior I had taken for granted turned out to be options LazyVim set internally. I was greeted on first launch by 8-space indents and a clipboard that would not survive a trip between terminal instances. So the first job was archaeology: I dug through LazyVim for every option I actually liked and copied them into config/options.lua. System clipboard, sensible folding via Treesitter (foldexpr = v:lua.vim.treesitter.foldexpr()), a global statusline, conceallevel for markup: the unglamorous foundation everything else sits on.

The plugin manager is lazy.nvim, the de facto standard, and it genuinely just works. The bootstrap snippet from their docs clones it on first run, and after that every file under lua/plugins/ that returns a spec table is imported automatically. No central manifest to keep in sync; a new file is a new plugin.

This is where the config diverged most sharply from where it started. The first pass used mason.nvim, mason-lspconfig, and nvim-lspconfig, the standard stack. All three are now gone. Neovim 0.11 ships a native LSP configuration API: vim.lsp.config defines a server and vim.lsp.enable turns it on, and any table returned from lsp/<name>.lua on the runtime path is picked up as that server's config. So core.lsp is just a list:

Each server then gets a plain Lua file in lsp/. No package manager, no bridge plugin translating between two config schemas. I install the servers themselves through my system package manager and let Neovim wire them up. It is dramatically less machinery for the same result, and when something breaks there is exactly one place to look.

The Python setup is the clearest upgrade. I dropped pyright for basedpyright and split responsibilities: basedpyright does type checking and inlay hints, while ruff runs as its own language server handling import organization and diagnostics. In the LazyVim days I fought constantly with import resolution, hand-writing a function to locate each project's virtualenv and pin pythonPath to its interpreter. basedpyright resolves environments well enough on its own that the hack is gone. clangd, texlab, and lua_ls round out the set, each configured in its own file. texlab in particular carries a fair amount of custom command wiring for building, forward search into Zathura, and environment manipulation.

A shared LspAttach autocommand in core.lsp binds the buffer-local LSP keymaps once, for every server: go-to-definition and friends route through fzf-lua pickers, and document highlighting, inlay-hint toggling, and native completion get enabled per-buffer based on what each client actually supports.

header.h2: Forester finally has a real language server

section.p: The original post described an ugly hack to get Forester completion. The forester.nvim plugin exposed a completion source, but only for nvim-cmp; blink.cmp (which I use; see below) needs a blink.compat shim, and that shim expected a plugin to be a source rather than to bury one inside a larger feature set. Getting reference completion working meant reading blink.compat internals and registering the source by hand.

None of that survives, because Forester now ships an actual language server. My lsp/forester.lua just launches forester lsp and hands it the forest root. The one wrinkle worth recording: forester locates the forest by its process working directory and ignores the LSP rootUri, and Neovim does not spawn the server in root_dir by default. So the config resolves the nearest forest.toml and starts the RPC process with an explicit cwd; otherwise the server exits with status 1 whenever Neovim's cwd has no forest.toml (e.g. when I open a tree from $HOME). Reference completion, indispensable for writing this very blog, now flows through the standard LSP path with no shim in sight.

Completion is blink.cmp, the successor that finally displaced nvim-cmp. Its sources are lsp, path, snippets, and omni, with LuaSnip as the snippet engine. Because I lean on native LSP, the on_attach handler calls vim.lsp.completion.enable with autotrigger, so the server's completions feed the picker directly.

Layered on top is supermaven-nvim for AI ghost-text suggestions: accept-suggestion, accept-word, and clear bound to <C-l>, <C-j>, and <C-]>. It fills the role Copilot-style tools play elsewhere without getting in the way of the structured LSP and snippet completions.

Going all the way back to the Gilles Castel blog post, I have always wanted snippets that auto-expand. Under LazyVim I had settled for friendly-snippets on native Neovim snippets; rebuilding from scratch, I refused to compromise. The engine is LuaSnip, which blink.cmp supports natively, and I have to plug the luasnip-latex-snippets repo that ports the original UltiSnips math snippets over. My own snippets live in a small local plugin, custom-luasnip-snippets.nvim, vendored under lua/local/.

The trick I had wanted for years and can finally do: load LaTeX math snippets while inside math environments in Forester. The snippet plugin runs with use_treesitter = true, so it inspects the Forester Treesitter grammar, finds the node types for math environments, and only expands the math snippets when the cursor is actually inside one. Writing \TeX inside a .tree file feels exactly like writing it in a .tex file.

Formatting runs through conform.nvim on save. Python is handled by ruff_format followed by pyink, Lua by stylua. This replaced the old black + isort pairing, folding most of it into the same ruff that already runs as a language server. Formatting falls back to the LSP formatter when no dedicated tool is configured for a filetype.

The fuzzy finder is fzf-lua, which replaced Telescope. File and grep pickers are scoped to a detected project root, which a small utils.root module (lifted from LazyVim) finds by walking LSP workspace folders, .git, and cwd. A dedicated tex override restricts live-grep to \TeX source files.

The piece I am most fond of is forester-new, a local plugin that wires the editor into the forest's own note pipeline. It shells out to scripts/new so every tree gets the standard frontmatter and routing, then commands like :ForesterNew, :ForesterStub, :ForesterCitek, and :ForesterTransient handle the follow-through: creating a tree and inserting a \transclude, stubbing a concept and dropping a [[id]] link at the cursor, or, in visual mode, lifting a selection into a new tree and replacing it in place with the transclude. Stub-and-link without ever leaving the sentence, which is exactly the friction the forest workflow is supposed to remove.

I originally built a whole in-editor Anki workflow on top of AnkiConnect and a vendored anki.nvim. That has since moved out of the editor and into the forest itself: cards are just \taxon{Card} trees, and scripts/anki-sync mirrors them into Anki, creating the note on first sync and updating in place thereafter. Writing a card is now the same as writing any other tree, snippets and all, and the sync is one command away. This is an example of a card.
